content: The pronunciation of English words on Wikipedia is typically provided using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA). This system is designed to ensure that the pronunciation can be understood regardless of the reader's dialect, which is why a broad transcription is generally employed. For a more comprehensive guide to the IPA, including sounds not found in English, refer to the Help:IPA section. This key includes standard pronunciations from American, British, and Australian English. However, not all distinctions presented will be relevant to every reader's dialect. For instance, if you pronounce cot and caught the same way, you can disregard the difference between the symbols used to represent these sounds. Similarly, in many dialects, certain IPA symbols only appear before vowels. If this applies to your speech, you can ignore those symbols in the pronunciation guides where they would not be pronounced. It is unnecessary to provide multiple transcriptions for such variations. For a more detailed use of the IPA to highlight differences between English dialects, to transcribe languages other than English, or if IPA symbols are not displayed correctly in your browser, additional resources are available at the bottom of the page. Key Notes: 1. Although the IPA symbol for a trill is technically distinct, it is often replaced with a simpler symbol in broad transcriptions of English. 2. Some dialects, such as Scottish and Southern American English, use certain IPA symbols that are pronounced differently in other varieties of English. 3. In most dialects, specific IPA symbols are pronounced the same way in certain contexts, such as in the words dew and do. 4. Most people pronounce Hawai‘i without the glottal stop sound represented in IPA. 5. It is debated whether English truly distinguishes between primary and secondary stress, but it is conventional to mark them as such in transcriptions. 6. For clarity, certain forms are preferred in transcription, even when there is debate about their accuracy (e.g., Glennallen). 7. American conventions often write certain unstressed vowels differently than British conventions, though some British sources, like the OED, have recently adopted the American style. 8. In many dialects, dew and do are pronounced the same, so only one transcription is typically shown in guides. 9. Due to American influence, schwas (unstressed vowel sounds) are often omitted in many Wikipedia articles. When they are included, distinctions may be transcribed analogously to vowels not followed by specific sounds. 10. Few British dictionaries distinguish certain sounds, though the OED uses a pseudo-IPA symbol for clarity.
